title: 25 Classroom Management Myths To Ponder This Summer summer/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a flurry of reader emails, Michael Linsin compiles 25 widely held classroom management myths that he argues serve mainly as ready-made excuses for unruliness and teacher struggles — beliefs such as needing to reward good behavior, requiring parent or administrative support, needing charisma to build rapport, or accepting that some talking during instruction is unavoidable. He frames the list as a summer reflection exercise rather than a fully explained rebuttal of each myth, pointing readers toward the site's larger archive for deeper treatment of individual topics. The piece closes by urging teachers to use the quieter summer months to honestly examine which of these embedded assumptions may be holding their classroom back. While concise, the list is framed with real explanatory context about why these myths persist and what purpose they serve for struggling teachers.
points: The article compiles 25 specific, commonly held classroom management myths, framed as ready-made excuses that justify teacher struggles and unruly behavior.
Myths span topics like rewards, roster luck, needing outside support, charisma, individual attention for difficult students, and stress being an inevitable part of the job.
The author frames these beliefs as deeply embedded in teaching culture and held onto reverently because they excuse rather than solve problems.
Readers are pointed to the site's broader 400+ article archive for deeper explanation of any individual myth listed.
Summer is framed as the ideal, lower-pressure time to reflect on which myths may be quietly limiting a teacher's classroom.
quotes: It occurred to me while responding to a recent flurry of emails just how prevalent the myths are surrounding classroom management.
They're held on to tightly, often reverently, by those who seek to justify their struggles.
So I present the 25 most common myths in the bright light of day.
My hope is that this list will help you identify those areas in need of improvement.
Individually, the myths may require further explanation, especially if you’re new to our website.
It’s important to periodically take a step back and gain some perspective, to reflect on where you are now and where you’d like to be.
